# A morning

In 1446, the book that introduced Hangeul (한글) opened by stating the entire
system in a few pages (every letter, every assembly rule) before a single
page of explanation. The scholars who wrote its postface made a claim about
that brevity: *the wise can learn these letters before the morning is over.*

This part makes the same claim. It is short on purpose, and it is meant to
be read in one sitting: a first plot, then the whole vocabulary on one page,
then practice (first reading plots other people wrote, then writing your
own, including your first refusals from the engine and what they teach).

Nothing in this part is exhaustive. Every idea you meet here has a full
chapter later in the book. The goal of the morning is different: when it is
over, no gog sentence anywhere (in this book, in a colleague's script)
should look foreign to you.
